utterances.text: Let me make sure I understand your position on this. The headquarters of the Bosnian Serb army operating in the Sarajevo theatre was not a legitimate target from the time that the UN placed personnel in those headquarters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any written agreement between the parties to that effect?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts was that agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The agreement was that we told both sides individually, because they wouldn't come together, to talk.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me stop you for a moment. I badly phrased my question. You've told us there was a written agreement to that effect. When was that written agreement made?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do you not have copies of the agreements?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you say it's in the heavy weapons agreement?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Did it strike you as odd that the headquarters for the Bosnian Serb forces were not a legitimate target but the same did not apply to the headquarters for the Bosnian Presidency forces?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had no people situated at the Bosnian Presidency forces headquarters. There were no military observers there.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I understand that. But looking back on it, does it not strike you as odd that the Bosnian Serb headquarters should be spared and not those of their enemy?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not spared.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it not strike you as odd that that situation was agreed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. The position that you had by July was that the UN personnel on the Bosnian Serb side were some distance from the confrontation lines; correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they were.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereas the headquarters in Sarajevo were, to use your earlier estimate, some 400 metres from the confrontation line; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were close, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When one looks at the video that you provided us, in particular of the Lukavica barracks, they appear on that video to be in generally good condition, don't they?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not actually true. What you see is yes, they are in good condition, but no, they were not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You don't see smashed windows and shards of glass lying about, do you?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You don't in the videos, no.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The impacts on Lukavica were far less, so it would seem, than impacts on and in the vicinity of the headquarters in the PTT building; would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, yesterday, you said this: "The Serbian forces were basically in Bosnia wanted to keep the land that they had for a long time, hundreds of years. The Muslims, on the other hand, on the Presidency side, or the Presidency side, wanted to totally cleanse Bosnia and Herzegovina of any Serbians and have a totally Muslim state."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is on public record --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please wait, I haven't asked you the question yet. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that fairly state your view, at this stage, as to the objectives of the two warring factions?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When did you first arrive at that conclusion?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I arrived at that conclusion after a consolidated media campaign by the Muslims against UNPROFOR, the UN, and the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And I take it that was when you were in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember the month?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: July.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when in the month of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't, but there is a article --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please -- if you could respond just to the question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If we need some more information, we'll ask for it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And make a pause as well.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I am sorry?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And make a pause as well before you answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You're not the first one to forget about it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A number of times over the last three days when you have been asked when things have happened, you've said July. Was July a turning point for you; yes or no?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From what perspective?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your view of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: July was a very busy month and you can have a look at any -- I mean you can look at all the documents I've got with me right now and that will show you that July was a very busy month.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it a turning point for you in terms of your view of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it probably was, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, apart from the media campaign that you've referred to, was there any other event in July that affected your view of the conflict in particular who was responsible for the conflict?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was targeted a number of times in July, specifically, and I mean it was by direct fire, it was not by indirect fire. Indirect fire was nothing, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. And yesterday you told us that you were targeted 13 times directly and personally, mostly by the Bosnian Muslim forces, as you call it, and on the other occasions, by the Croatian forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say personally targeted, do you mean that they wanted to kill Richard Gray?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, they did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: They were targeting you not as a UN worker but as Richard Gray?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had two death threats to me, one to my face, and one by telephone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: And on at least one occasion, I informed the liaison officers who were present in the PTT and I told them exactly when and where I was going and when I went there, I was machine-gunned.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we don't have time to take you through each of those 13 incidents, but just to be clear on this, you're saying that on each of the occasions that you were shot at, you are convinced that the shooter wanted to kill you because you are Richard Gray; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were shooting -- in most cases, they were shooting at a UN vehicle, on at least two occasions, they knew it was Richard Gray, okay, but they -- I mean it was full daylight in a large APC and on one particular occasion, they knew I was in the vehicle and they shot at me with a 50 calibre machine-gun in broad daylight with bright sunshine in summer, 8 tonne APC, UN markings, flags flying, you couldn't mistake us. We called the UN marking on the side of the APC a target.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, that's a little different from what you said a few minutes ago and I want to be clear on this. Are you now saying that on at least two occasions, you're convinced that you were targeted as Richard Gray but on the other occasions, you were targeted because you happened to be in a UN-marked vehicle?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct, yeah, that's true.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, we've heard evidence from a number of UN personnel who were there during the conflict and suffice to say it was a very disturbing experience, there's no doubt about that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you, after -- I will withdraw that. Mr. President, at this stage could we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We'll turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I'll repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me take you back to the words that you told us yesterday as to your understanding of what motivated the Serb and the Bosnian government forces in the Sarajevo conflict. And I suggest to you that your view is a little one-sided.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would disagree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us over the last two days of an incident involving Lord Carrington. I suggest to you that you are incorrect, firstly, as to the identity of the politician involved, and secondly, as to the date. What would you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: You could be correct on the identity of the politician and the date, I would have to check on, but I think it was -- it was a British politician, it was either Lord Carrington or it was the foreign secretary for the UK.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you say you have to check on the date, do you remember that when you first told us about it you did just that, you took out your diary and you checked the date? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And having checked the date, you told us it was the 3rd of July, 1992. I suggest to you that on the 3rd of July, 1992, indeed, Lord Carrington arrived in Sarajevo. I suggest to you there was no mortaring incident during that visit.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, there was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a mortar incident.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And you have --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: During his visit.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you have a note of that mortaring incident during his visit?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't have a note of it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Well, on the tape that you provided us, was there a BBC news report about the visit by Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't recall everything that was on the tape. I mean there are four or five tapes that I provided.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If there was -- I withdraw that. Perhaps the Defence might agree that there is a report of the Lord Carrington visit.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I think that we can, in fact, see this politician in one of the video sequences but I don't know whether the dates correspond because I only had a very short time to look at it so in fact, yes, I believe it was Lord Carrington.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand that the Defence agrees that there is a video picture where a person which you recognise as Lord Carrington appears without knowing the date. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If it happened as you tell it -- I withdraw that. Did General MacKenzie go with Lord Carrington to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Have you read General MacKenzie's account, published account of his time in Sarajevo, entitled "Peacekeeper, the Road to Sarajevo"?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have a personally signed copy of it in which I appear many times.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And do you remember that he wrote about the visit of Lord Carrington?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you accept from me that in his account, he made no mention of any mortar incident?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will accept that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the other hand, Sir Douglas Hurd --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, that's the guy. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Sarajevo --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the 17th of July?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, that's him.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And there was a mortar incident at the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was him. He was a foreign secretary, right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. We've got it. That's the one.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And this was the incident that you described as a goody?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry, a what?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: A goody.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't good at all.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were your words when you first talked about it. This was a goody. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't. And if I did say that, I withdraw it and I'm very sorry. Because it wasn't good at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I would like to know where, could we have the reference, where was this quoted from, could Mr. Ierace give the reference.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The transcript for the 18th of February time 18.17 and 43 seconds on my transcript, answer: "Okay this is a goody. Okay. We had a visit of Lord Carrington on the 3rd of July, 1992."

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you now think that you got the date wrong?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I recall very well that moment when this "goody" arrived.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You may ask questions about it. If you are telling us that in your view, "goody" might have reflected to something else as to the event, you are certainly allowed to ask questions to that extent.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't have to. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you now think -- I withdraw that. That your memory has been significantly affected as to the events that took place in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember everything totally vividly and my memory may be affected by the fact that they happened 11 years ago and I don't have a total written record of the events, I only have a record of some or most of the events, but my memory of what actually happened can never, ever be altered.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How many mortars were there that fell that day at the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were two bombs that landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Something you would never forget?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never and it's on videotape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The videotape that you gave us?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The videotape doesn't have the mortars landing, does it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it does not, it has the aftermath.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember when you read General MacKenzie's account he said there were ten mortar rounds that landed immediately across the street from the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall that but I know that in the meeting, while we were having the meeting, there were mortar bombs landing so, I mean, his recollection may be that there were two and then there were eight, but I mean, there were -- there were mortar bombs landing while the meeting was actually going on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay. I'll read you his version: "On Douglas Hurd's arrival, there were 10 to 15 members of the TDF on either side of the building's entrance as a sort of honour guard".

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would you slow down please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Once he had entered the main door, the group of TDF on the right of the entrance joined their colleagues on the left and the entire group walked around to the west side of the building and took cover." I'll stop there for a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. One refers normally to the quotation taken from a book which was -- which I presume should have been copied so we should have it to know what is the context and I believe this is the minimum that we can ask for.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will provide copies.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, I do understand that you get the context.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, just stopping there for a moment, the other day you told us that you were out the front and the police -- I'm now quoting "actually moved inside the building and left me standing outside the front."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's incorrect. What I said was they moved from the left to the right and there were two armed soldiers, they weren't police, they were just armed soldiers. They moved inside the building and left me standing out the front and the soldiers or the -- rather the police at the very front who were across the opposite side of the road, they moved from the left to the right, then the bombs landed and then the ambulance was there, then --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, please. I'm not making this up. I am reading the transcript. I'll read you the full sentences of your words two days ago.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, okay, fine.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "An ambulance arrived no longer than 30 seconds after the bombs had landed"

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "The police moved back. I was standing in the entrance with liaison officers from the Bosnian Presidency. They actually moved inside the building and left me standing outside the front".

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "Which I thought was really nice when the bombs actually landed because they knew they were coming."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. And then the police moved back to where they were when the ambulance arrived and they had all the media there and then Douglas Hurd arrived and it was all mayhem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE NIETO-NAVIA
utterances.text: Mr. Ierace, I think you should read before -- start before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, thank you, Your Honour. I'll read the -- earlier and I correct myself, Mr. Gray.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: "There was then a delay and so he was 30 minutes late in actually getting to the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, not only would I like to have it slowed down, but this is very characteristic. These copies were ready and yet we were not given so that early enough to be able to go through them which I really do not understand. I have to read this, I cannot concentrate on this. I am reading it, let us allow us to read it slowly and then we shall take it up again slowly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Reading the transcript of the 18th and if you would please do it slowly, Mr. -- "You started and then there was then a delay and so he was 30 minutes late." Yes, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: "In actually getting to the Presidency to meet the Bosnian Muslim, whatever Presidency side. They had very carefully placed out a cordon of police which stretched down the opposite side from the Presidency and the police were set at 10 metre intervals, et cetera. We were told that he was late and that was fine, I mean, it was UN time, and then we were told he was coming. The police moved as I was looking from the front of the Presidency. They were -- they moved from left to right. Immediately after that, and while he was actually on his way, two mortar bombs landed, 82 millimetre mortar bombs, and I know the difference between 82, 120, 122, 105, I've been through it, they landed and they killed people and wounded people right there. An ambulance arrived no longer than 30 seconds after the bombs had landed. The police moved back. I was standing in the entrance with liaison officers from the Bosnian Presidency. They actually moved inside the building and left me standing outside the front which I thought was really nice." Who moved inside the building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The two liaison officers moved inside the building. The police on the opposite side of the road moved to -- from left to right, as I looked at them from the front entrance of the Presidency and when the bombs had landed, the ambulance had arrived, they moved back and the two liaison officers came out from inside the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you see anything sinister in the two liaison officers having gone inside?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They knew the bombs were going to land.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The fact that they went inside by itself was not conclusive of that, was it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: To me, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The distinguished guest had moved inside?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, he hadn't.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had other -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where was he at that stage that the bombs --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He had not arrived. He was about to drive through where the mortars landed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, was General MacKenzie with Sir Douglas Hurd at the stage that the bombs fell as far as you knew?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, as far as I knew he normally travelled in a VBL which is a small French armoured personnel carrier, as opposed to a VAB which is a large one, which I normally travelled in, and he arrived in the small one and Douglas Hurd and his entourage.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please slow down for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Douglas Hurd arrived in the larger APC with his entourage. They all got out. There was pandemonium going on 100 metres away where the casualties were being taken away to the hospital and that was that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you can remember being out the front with the pandemonium and Sir Douglas Hurd arriving; is that right?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And General MacKenzie?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: No doubt at that stage, security officers running everywhere trying to get them into the building, I take it?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They got out of the vehicles and they were basically shepherded into the building.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Right. Mr. Presidency, might I just clarify whether the witness has a copy of the excerpt. Do you have --

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, I've got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please turn to the second page. It has number 457 in the top right hand corner.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, got it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: This is a photocopy of a page from General MacKenzie's book.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I didn't have enough time to read. What are we talking about?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We're talking about a copy of the book, page 457, a book of which the title is "Peacekeeper".

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I haven't had the time to read it fully. Well, I -- can I have this time to do this? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I think generally, when a document comes up during cross-examination, if you need more time to read it before you re-examine the witness, you certainly will have it but if you could do that, if it would help you to take one minute or one minute and a half to get a general impression, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, could you please read it to yourself from the entry July 17 to the bottom of the page and the end of the first paragraph on the following page, that is, the first two lines of the following page as well and tell me when you've done that.

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Apart from the sequence.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well first of all, have you finished reading that section?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Including over the page?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Has my learned colleague read it?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I've already underlined it, yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now, do you agree on this account, Douglas Hurd had arrived and was inside the building at the time that the mortars fell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The mortars fell --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Please, I'm asking you whether you agree that's what this account says?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you accept that Sir Douglas Hurd was inside the building with General MacKenzie at the time the mortars fell?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I accept that some of the mortars fell while they were inside the building but there were two mortar bombs that landed before they arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: If that's the case, Mr. Gray, given that you gave evidence about this topic on three separate occasions over the last two days, why did you not tell us that more than two mortar bombs fell? Why did you not say to us that two fell before he arrived and more fell while he was in the building?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. In relation to the end of Mr. Ierace's sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Do you consider it to be an incorrect statement of what --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In relation to what the witness has said, we're really on the razor's edge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, the question was at least I'll rephrase it in such a way that why did you not say to us - that was the question of Mr. Ierace - that two fell before the arrival and more fell afterwards.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because I wasn't asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Where were you when the other -- sorry, how many fell whilst Sir Douglas Hurd was inside the building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't keeping count. Counting mortar bombs and counting shells, for me, anyway, had long gone.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you hear the primaries firing with these other eight mortar shells?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, you can't. I was inside the building. But when I was outside the building I could hear the primaries firing.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the time that the other eight fell, you were inside the building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Whereabouts inside the building?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Inside the conference room on the second floor.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And do you remember counting eight shells?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you I didn't --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sorry, I withdraw that. How do you know that there were eight shells?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you I didn't count them.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. But do you know now how many there were?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How far apart did they land, in other words, did they all land however many there were, in the same instant or over a period of seconds or minutes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Over a period of minutes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, this is a -- an incident of extraordinary magnitude, isn't it, that all these mortar shells landed some before and some while the English -- the British foreign secretary was inside the Presidency?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. And how many people do you remember were killed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't see the people who were killed while we were actually in the meeting because they were -- had been removed when we came out from the meeting. So I didn't know how many were actually killed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find it odd that there were -- that ambulances attended so quickly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found it extremely -- well, it was beyond circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. There is a redundant "s" in the question of Mr. Ierace. Mr. Ierace should refer to the witness' statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I don't follow that, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I think you were talking in the plural, but as Mr. -- It's the recollection of Mr. Piletta-Zanin that the witness testified about singular form of ambulance. It's -- do you understand what I mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you find it odd that the ambulance arrived so quickly? I'm sorry. I will withdraw that because I think you've already answered it. I think you said: "I found it extremely -- well, it was beyond circumstance."

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did it not occur to you that there might have been another explanation that given the history of Sarajevo over the previous months and given the importance of the occasion, it would be quite appropriate for the government authorities to have ambulances, if not in close proximity, even there should they be required that there was hardly a safe area?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not. With all the previous visits, there had never been an ambulance close by, never.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Well, how do you know that if, as you know accept, there wasn't a similar incident when Lord Carrington arrived? How -- to explain my question further, how do you know that if there hadn't been mortars arriving at the Presidency when he was there, that an ambulance wouldn't have appeared promptly?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no idea, but the coincidence was -- I mean it had got so bad with these sorts of incidences with people like President Mitterand and Carrington and Hurd and a number of others had got so bad, we actually were running a sweepstake on this particular arrival on when, to the second, the mortar bombs would land. That is how bad it was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, do you remember I asked you a question about the arrival of an ambulance and suggested to you that you had taken only one of a number of possible explanations?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is true, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What has your answer got to do with that question?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was no reason to have -- it was a quiet, quiet day. There was no reason to have -- ambulances had other business to do. It was very quiet day and there was no reason to have one pre-positioned for what happened.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Sir, in the months that preceded this visit, there were many quiet times, I suggest to you, otherwise quiet times, when mortar shells would land out of the blue anywhere in Sarajevo. What do you say to that?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: True.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it not prudent for the government authorities to ensure that if required, ambulances could attend as soon as possible?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is a possibility.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Look at again please at the passage you just read and do you agree there is no mention in this account of two mortar shells landing before Sir Douglas Hurd entered the building; do you agree?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I agree.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I suggest to you it didn't happen, that mortar shells landed after he entered the building and not before?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Review the videotape, I can show you if you like, I can do it after this I can show you exactly the sequence and where the mortar bombs landed, exactly, precisely. They landed. I saw them with my own eyes. Two mortar bombs landed. There was a gentleman in his late 50s, early 60s, he was standing --

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Understand this, please, I'm not disputing --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President, I think under the circumstances it would be very useful if the witness could make a precise -- make his answer very precise for everybody, for the Chamber, for the Prosecution, for the Defence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: I will press what I respectfully say is my right to make clear to the witness what's in dispute and what's not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think what the witness explained was not in a direct answer to what Mr. Ierace asked him but on the other hand, Mr. Gray, when you told us about what you saw, did you want to tell us about anything that would be in your mind still of what happened or something that would prove that it was before the politician arrived that the mortar fell?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The proof, Your Honour, is on the videotape and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. But if you are talking about a at a certain age then of course as such, I mean, could be before or after the politician had arrived. Is there any specific fact you would like to tell us which indicates that it was before the arrival that the shells landed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is my word that they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I do understand. Please proceed, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did you discuss this incident with General MacKenzie after Sir Douglas Hurd left?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And did you tell him what you saw and what you heard?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there any other UN officer in the front of the Presidency at the time that the two mortar shells landed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it follow that General MacKenzie was dependent entirely on your account in terms of UN sources as to what happened when the first two shells landed?

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection, Mr. President. I cannot really phrase it but it has to do with the structure of observation at various places because we have already seen a large number of documents and therefore, this question is quite redundant and that is why I am objecting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Of course the witness could have answered that, again, Mr. Piletta-Zanin, in your objections you should not give the clues to what you think that would -- could you please answer the question, witness.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, can you repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray-- yes. Mr. Ierace will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does it follow that you were the only UN officer on the scene at the time and you spoke to General MacKenzie afterwards that General MacKenzie was dependent entirely on your account as far as you know, in terms of UN sources, as to what happened when the first two shells landed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was dependent on my account and his recollection, which -- I mean, he was an extremely busy person, obviously, I was busy as well, but, I mean, he recalled the mortar bombs that landed during the meeting but he didn't physically see the two bombs that landed just before he arrived.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So he had to depend on you, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Now did you tell him that people were killed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: And that's something that was obvious to you, was it, when two mortar shells landed that people had been killed?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was 100 metres away. It's on the videotape.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We'll come to that. Did you see people who had been killed at the time?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. President, I'd like the videotape to be played. I've prepared a tape which has a number of segments on it and this is the first one. Perhaps the witness's screen could be put on the appropriate --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but, Mr. Ierace, we've got three minutes left on the clock I take it you would have some questions for the witness related to that videotape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: How much time would that take.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: It takes -- it takes less than three minutes, I think, about three minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then we'll play the videotape.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, if you speak very -- let's just first view the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection to all the questions relative to this tape. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I could not hear you. I don't know whether the interpreters could hear Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will repeat, objection formally, formal objection to all the questions that the Prosecution might want to ask as usual in relation to this tape and that is under our rules. Well, the Prosecution has not bothered to provide a transcript so that that transcript could be translated for the General so that the General could know what this is about. The General didn't understand anything about it. They enter the -- the Prosecution will be asking questions about the text about which General Galic knows nothing and that is -- that does not really do. I know we are pressed by the time, the General Galic simply does not know anything what is on this tape, anything about this text and that is not natural, that you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, what can I say? The Defence played excerpts yesterday and didn't -- I didn't object, obviously didn't have any problem with that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We haven't had the tapes for very long. In an ideal world we would provide transcripts of course. That's hardly the fault of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The Defence takes the position that it's different for the Defence and apart from that, they explained to General Galic what the tape was about. Are you willing to explain what the tape was about?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then please proceed.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On the tape that we have just viewed, did we see, firstly, --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I take note, I thank you, but I can see that this is not going to be sufficient. The information is not sufficient for the defendant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Perhaps the -- let me just confer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Would the interpreters be able to, upon replay, to translate the comment we hear on this tape?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it is too fast.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Mr. President, from the B/C/S booth it would be extremely difficult because of the speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I did listen to number three because -- which gives no interpretation at all. Could I please be informed whether this is...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, the text is too fast and we need to see either the text or view the tapes several times over.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the Prosecution is invited to make a transcript of the tape and then it could be replayed tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that places the Prosecution in an impossible position. I understand the principles involved.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: We're now sitting at 9.00 a.m., I have a number of passages of tape. We're informed this is a problem at 7.00. I don't have the staff to do that. If it's possible to see it tomorrow afternoon, then we can do it tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Are we just talking about the comment of this tape or are there other tapes to be played, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Other tapes as well, Mr. President. Mr. President, in the normal course of events we would have received this material from the Defence a long time before we did and the Prosecution has time and again in relation to this witness done its best to accommodate the problems of the Defence and this now places a requirement that we just can't meet on such short notice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The tapes have been provided at a very late stage, that means that this might result in a decision that we would have to sit tomorrow in the afternoon rather than tomorrow morning so that at least some time -- we try to solve it in a different way that's not possible. Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Very respectfully, I suggest that the argument of not sufficient personnel is not really reasonable. We all have to work in difficult conditions sometimes and I think we have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Piletta-Zanin, we all know the circumstances, we all know that there are teams that -- so that's something that is apparent to everyone we all know that the tapes arrived late no one is being blamed for it but just whether the argument is good or not, the main issue is how we solve this matter at the one hand. The --

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, very simply, if Mr. Ierace can write down the content of these tapes, and then give them to the booth, would that be such a difficult problem for Mr. Ierace? I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The question is Mr. Piletta-Zanin puts the question to you whether it would be a great effort and whether there would be a possibility to write down the text of the videos that you are still about to play?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: But we're now at 9.00 in the morning, Mr. President, yes. We've got 16 minutes of footage and I just don't have the staff to do that tonight. And obviously I have my own tasks to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: In relation to cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What would be the earliest time you would be able to have finished this transcript of 16 minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, I imagine, 10.30. I should indicate of course we've given a copy of the tape to the Defence but 10.30 in the morning. We should be able to do an English copy by then, in terms of a translated copy that would take longer, obviously.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but once we have text or part of text they could be translated, I take it, to the accused in one way or the other. Would you have -- I do understand that if you are required now to provide this text that it would interrupt your cross-examination at this very moment and -- would you have subjects to cover that time or would you say then we have to start at 10.30?

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Perhaps a compromise, Mr. President, if we were to start at 10.00, I'd certainly have material that I could utilise in the first half hour. The problem is simply that we might end up with a somewhat jumbled cross-examination if I can't go methodically through it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Piletta-Zanin.

utterances.speaker: MR. PILETTA-ZANIN
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. I apologise but on this subject, we have another problem. We promised a transcript of our tape that was looked at yesterday but the tape is still in the hands of the registry, I believe, so I don't know how we are going to do -- to find exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... Let's first try to deal with the problem we are faced with at this very moment. The parties should be prepared that we will sit tomorrow in the afternoon but Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the Chamber is aware that all the schedules have been changed so what we'll try to do is to see whether we can sit -- change it again to tomorrow in the afternoon so that we have the full time of sitting tomorrow available to us. If not possible, the parties should be prepared to start at 10.00 in the morning but first option of the Chamber is, if possible, to move to the afternoon. If not possible, the parties should keep themself informed to start at 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ierace.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: An alternative proposal to accommodate everyone, if we start at 9.00, if by 9.00 we have an English transcription of the first segment, then I can at least proceed with evidence in -- cross-examination in relation to that incident we'll keep them coming into the courtroom through the morning and I'll --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And then the written text can be translated by the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If that would solve the problem then we'll -- yes, Mr. Gray, you are waiting. What would you like to tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm just saying that the piece of videotape that the Prosecution have shown is very good. It's shown from one particular angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we are not at this moment, Mr. Gray, the interpreters have been suffering already from 15 minutes where we finished late also yesterday. Once --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There is another piece of videotape there which is taken from the other angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I do understand but it's up to the parties to show those videos to the Court that they deem of importance.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, that is important. Question about that because I'm not aware of any other part of the tape that relates to this incident.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, there is, it shows a brown Mercedes car, okay, and that is immediately when the two first mortar bombs landed. It was taken directly from the Presidency side of -- I mean -- the tape you showed was coming from the PTT side.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could just ask a question to hurry things along.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Mr. Gray, I've shown you all of that component?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: But it's on a different tape and it's taken from a different angle by a different crew.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There are four tapes, if we can speak slowly, two of BBC tapes, is it one of those two tapes?

utterances.speaker: RICHARD PAUL GRAY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean I'd have to look at it. I mean I could find it for you. There's no problem about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IERACE
utterances.text: The trouble is, Mr. President, I need those tapes tonight to locate a final segment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: What we face at this very moment is the consequences of something no one is to blame for is the late arrival of videotapes. Let's see how far we come, that means we start tomorrow morning at 9.00. We have the English transcript of the first episode to be shown available so that it can be translated and the subsequent footages will drop in consequently and if there's any other Mercedes or whatever footage to be played, we'll see. The Chamber is not very much inclined to try to rush into the weekend and all parties are suffering from late arrival; therefore, we should proceed cautiously. We'll adjourn until tomorrow morning 9.00 - with again the apologies to the technical staff and the interpreters - in courtroom 2 and may I instruct you, Mr. Gray, not to speak with anyone, not the parties, not anyone else, about your testimony in this court and we'd like to see you back tomorrow morning at 9.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: at 7.17 p.m. to be reconvened on Friday, the 21st day of February 2003 at 9.00 a.m. 17 18 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
